summary: Carbenicillin is an extended-spectrum (antipseudomonal) carboxypenicillin. The oral form, carbenicillin indanyl sodium (Geocillin), is an acid-stable indanyl ester that is hydrolyzed to active carbenicillin after absorption; because oral doses produce only low blood levels but high urinary concentrations, it was used to treat urinary tract infections and prostatitis caused by susceptible Gram-negative organisms including Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus, E. coli and enterococci. The parenteral disodium salt was used systemically for serious Gram-negative and antipseudomonal infections. Carbenicillin is now discontinued in the United States (no current FDA-approved product) and has been largely superseded by ureidopenicillins (e.g., piperacillin) and other agents. As a beta-lactam it can cause hypersensitivity (including anaphylaxis), and the disodium form carries a substantial sodium load relevant in cardiac/renal patients.
indications: Acute and chronic urinary tract infections (cystitis, pyelonephritis) caused by susceptible E. coli, Proteus species (including indole-positive), Enterobacter and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (oral indanyl form)
Prostatitis caused by susceptible E. coli, Proteus mirabilis, Enterobacter and enterococci (Streptococcus faecalis) (oral indanyl form)
Serious systemic Gram-negative and antipseudomonal infections - septicemia, respiratory, soft tissue, intra-abdominal and genitourinary infections (parenteral disodium form, historical)

admin: Oral indanyl tablets may be taken with or without food; swallow with adequate fluid
Obtain urine/blood cultures and susceptibility testing before and during therapy
Reserve oral indanyl carbenicillin for urinary tract infections and prostatitis - it does NOT achieve therapeutic systemic blood levels
Parenteral disodium carbenicillin is given by IV infusion (or deep IM for lower doses); account for its high sodium content
Inquire about prior penicillin/cephalosporin/beta-lactam allergy before administration
moa: Carbenicillin is a bactericidal beta-lactam antibiotic. Its carboxyl side chain extends activity to many Gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas aeruginosa and indole-positive Proteus. Like other penicillins it binds penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibits the transpeptidation/cross-linking step of bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan synthesis, leading to cell wall weakening, autolysin activation and bacterial lysis. The oral indanyl ester is microbiologically inactive itself; after absorption it is rapidly hydrolyzed to free carbenicillin, which is then excreted in high concentration in the urine.

absolute: History of serious hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis) to carbenicillin or any penicillin
relative: History of allergy, especially to cephalosporins (possible cross-reactivity)
Significant renal impairment (oral form ineffective; parenteral accumulates)
Sodium-restricted states - congestive heart failure, severe hypertension (sodium load of disodium form)
Bleeding tendency / concurrent anticoagulants (platelet dysfunction at high doses)
History of GI disease such as colitis
monitor: Renal, hepatic and hematopoietic function during prolonged or high-dose therapy
Serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium) with parenteral high-dose therapy
Coagulation/bleeding time with high parenteral doses

preg: Penicillins, including carbenicillin, are generally regarded as acceptable in pregnancy and have a long record of use without evidence of fetal harm; carbenicillin was assigned former US Pregnancy Category B. Reproduction studies did not show impaired fertility or fetal harm, but adequate well-controlled human studies are lacking, so it should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Carbenicillin is excreted into breast milk in low concentrations. As with other penicillins, it is generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; observe the infant for diarrhea, candidiasis (thrush), rash or sensitization.
renal: Carbenicillin is eliminated principally by the kidneys. In renal impairment the oral indanyl ester fails to achieve adequate urinary concentrations and is not recommended when creatinine clearance falls below about 10 mL/min. For the parenteral disodium form, doses must be reduced and intervals lengthened in renal impairment to avoid accumulation, neurotoxicity (seizures) and electrolyte/sodium overload; carbenicillin is removed by hemodialysis.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment. Transient elevations of AST (SGOT) and other liver enzymes have been reported, occasionally with mild hepatitis-like findings; monitor liver function during prolonged therapy. No specific dose adjustment is routinely defined for hepatic impairment.

major: Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin) - synergistic antipseudomonal activity but physical/chemical inactivation if mixed in the same solution; high carbenicillin levels can inactivate aminoglycosides, especially in renal failure
Anticoagulants / antiplatelet agents - additive bleeding risk from carbenicillin-induced platelet dysfunction at high doses
moderate: Probenecid - decreases renal tubular secretion, raising and prolonging serum carbenicillin levels
Methotrexate - penicillins may reduce its renal clearance, increasing toxicity
Bacteriostatic antibiotics (tetracyclines, chloramphenicol) - may antagonize bactericidal penicillin activity
minor: Oral contraceptives - theoretical reduced efficacy (low evidence)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; no clinically significant food effect on the oral indanyl ester
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction is documented; alcohol is best avoided during active infection
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction (Clinitest) methods; can transiently elevate AST/liver enzymes; high concentrations may interfere with aminoglycoside assays

serious: Hypersensitivity reactions including urticaria, angioedema and anaphylaxis
Bleeding/hemorrhage from platelet dysfunction (high parenteral doses)
Electrolyte disturbance - hypernatremia from sodium load, hypokalemia (parenteral)
Neurotoxicity / seizures with very high doses or renal failure (parenteral)
rare: Transient elevation of AST/SGOT and other liver enzymes
emergency: Severe cutaneous reaction (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / exfoliative dermatitis)
Severe or bloody diarrhea suggesting C. difficile colitis

monitoring: Urine and/or blood cultures with susceptibility testing before and during therapy
Renal function (especially with parenteral form and in renal impairment)
Liver function tests on prolonged therapy
Complete blood count and signs of bleeding with high-dose parenteral use
Serum sodium and potassium with parenteral disodium form
Signs of hypersensitivity and superinfection (thrush, diarrhea, C. difficile)
counsel: Take the medicine exactly as prescribed and complete the full course even if you feel better
Tell your doctor about any past allergy to penicillins, cephalosporins or other antibiotics before starting
Stop the drug and seek urgent care for rash, swelling of face/lips/tongue, wheezing or trouble breathing
Report severe or watery/bloody diarrhea, which may occur during or even weeks after treatment
Drink plenty of fluids; this medicine is used mainly for urinary and prostate infections
A bad taste, nausea or loose stools may occur and are usually mild
pk: Bactericidal activity begins after absorption and hydrolysis of the indanyl ester to active carbenicillin
Peak serum levels about 0.5-1 hour after an oral dose; serum levels are low but urinary levels are high
Short-acting; therapeutic urinary concentrations maintained with four-times-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 C / 68-77 F); protect tablets from moisture
pearls: DISCONTINUED IN THE US - no current FDA-approved carbenicillin product; included for historical and reference completeness
Extended-spectrum (antipseudomonal) carboxypenicillin - one of the first penicillins with reliable activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and indole-positive Proteus
Oral indanyl ester (Geocillin) gives low blood but high URINARY levels, so it was used only for UTIs and prostatitis, not systemic infection
Parenteral disodium carbenicillin was the antipseudomonal/systemic form and carries a high sodium load - caution in heart failure and renal impairment
Largely superseded by ureidopenicillins (piperacillin) and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations; high doses can cause platelet dysfunction and bleeding
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule - do not double up. Spacing doses as evenly as possible helps keep effective drug levels and prevent resistance; complete the entire prescribed course.
overdose: Overdose may cause exaggerated adverse effects, chiefly neuromuscular hyperexcitability or seizures (particularly with high parenteral doses or in renal failure), and electrolyte disturbances. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring of renal function, electrolytes and neurological status, anticonvulsants for seizures, and discontinuation of the drug. Carbenicillin can be removed by hemodialysis.
